query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Microalloying equiatomic CoCrFeNi with a small amount of Ti (approximately 4–6 at.% Ti) will enable an adaptive, sliding-induced TiOx Magnéli-phase tribofilm in oxidizing environments that maintains a low coefficient of friction and wear rate from room temperature to 800 °C relative to the starting CoCrFeNi, by providing a low-shear, self-replenishing oxide layer at elevated temperatures and increased near-surface hardness at lower temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy, FCC, solutionized/homogenized, uncoated, tested in pin-on-disk sliding.
generation.intervention: Introduce 4–6 at.% Ti into the CoCrFeNi matrix (forming CoCrFeNi–Ti_x) via microalloying, keeping processing otherwise identical to the baseline.
generation.conditions: Sliding in dry air (oxidizing, RH < 20%), against an inert ceramic counterface (e.g., Al2O3 or Si3N4), sliding speed ~0.1 m/s, normal load 5–15 N, temperatures spanning 25–800 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: A continuous or near-continuous tribochemically formed TiOx Magnéli-phase-rich film (e.g., Ti4O7/Ti3O5) on the wear track, coexisting with mixed spinel oxides from the base alloy (e.g., Co–Cr spinels) that anchor the film; near-surface hardened layer due to Ti-induced solid solution strengthening and oxidation.
generation.mechanism: Under sliding in oxidizing atmospheres at elevated temperatures, Ti in the alloy is selectively oxidized and reduced under contact to oxygen-deficient TiOx Magnéli phases with layered structures and low shear strength, forming a self-replenishing, glaze-like tribofilm that reduces interfacial shear and adhesion. The mixed Co/Cr spinel oxides nucleated from the matrix stabilize and anchor this tribofilm. At lower temperatures, Ti microalloying increases near-surface hardness and reduces plowing and adhesive wear, limiting friction and wear until Magnéli phases become the dominant mediator as temperature rises.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to baseline CoCrFeNi, the Ti-microalloyed material will show a directional decrease in steady-state friction and wear across 25–800 °C in dry air. The friction reduction is expected to be modest at room temperature and strengthen with temperature, becoming significant from ~400 to 800 °C (on the order of tens of percent reduction). Wear rate will decrease across the full range, with the largest reductions at elevated temperatures due to the protective tribofilm.
generation.baseline: As-cast/solutionized equiatomic CoCrFeNi tested under the same sliding conditions (counterface, load, speed, atmosphere, temperature) without Ti microalloying.
generation.boundary: Effectiveness depends on an oxidizing environment and a chemically inert counterface; reduced or absent in vacuum or strongly reducing atmospheres where tribo-oxide formation is suppressed. Benefits may diminish below ~250–300 °C if Magnéli phases do not form, and at very high contact pressures (>~20 N in the stated geometry) or high speeds (>~0.2 m/s) that cause film spallation. Counterface materials that catalyze different tribochemistry (e.g., reactive steels) may alter performance.
generation.uncertainty: Direct evidence in CoCrFeNi for Ti-driven Magnéli-phase tribofilms across 25–800 °C was not evaluated here; the magnitude of friction reduction at room temperature is uncertain and may be small. Phase stability of CoCrFeNi–Ti_x and potential formation of brittle phases under specific processing routes could affect outcomes. The exact temperature onset and continuity of Magnéli-phase formation depend on oxygen availability, sliding conditions, and Ti content.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two materials: (1) baseline equiatomic CoCrFeNi and (2) CoCrFeNi–5 at.% Ti, both solutionized and polished identically. Conduct pin-on-disk tests in dry air against Al2O3 pins at 25, 200, 400, 600, and 800 °C; normal load 10 N; sliding speed 0.1 m/s; sliding distance 500 m at each temperature. After testing, characterize wear tracks by Raman spectroscopy and XPS to detect TiOx Magnéli phases and mixed spinel oxides; measure steady-state friction and volumetric wear rate by 3D profilometry.
measurements: Average steady-state coefficient of friction at each temperature (after run-in).
Volumetric wear rate (mm^3/N·m) of the disk at each temperature.
Raman/XPS identification of Magnéli-phase signatures (e.g., Ti4O7/Ti3O5) and mixed spinels on wear tracks.
Cross-sectional SEM/EDS of wear-track glaze to assess continuity and thickness.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if, at any temperature within 400–800 °C under the stated conditions, the Ti-microalloyed alloy fails to reduce the average steady-state friction by at least ~20% and the wear rate by at least ~30% relative to baseline, and/or if Magnéli-phase signatures are absent or non-dominant in the tribofilm; additionally, if room-temperature friction is higher than baseline by >10% without a compensating wear-rate reduction, the claim of wide-range improvement is falsified.
